newsitem.title: USA: Mystery of who hit Dan Rather may be solved.
newsitem.headline: Mystery of who hit Dan Rather may be solved.

text.p: A mystery that was the inspiration for a rock song -- who bashed CBS anchorman Dan Rather on the head after asking "What's the frequency Kenneth?" -- appears to have been solved.

Rather was beaten by a deranged man who went on to murder someone outside a television studio because voices in his head told him the networks were out to get him, according to the anchorman and an investigation by the New York Daily News.

Rather, after examining photographs provided by the Daily News, identified his assailant as William Tager, 49, who is serving a 25-year sentence for murdering NBC technican Campbell Theron Montgomery in front of the "Today" show studio in Rockefeller Centre in 1994.
Tager, a motorcycle dealer from North Carolina, drove up to the studio and started spraying people with bullets from an automatic rifle. Montgomery died trying to shield others.

"I'm grateful that the mystery has been solved," Rather said in a statement, adding: "What happened to me is not important. What is important is the tragedy of Campbell Theron Montgomery, who was killed trying to save the lives of others. Our attention should be on his memory and his family."
The news of Rather's beating was treated as a major event when it took place on Oct. 4, 1986. It was front-page news then and, nearly 11 years later, the saga has not gone away.

Rather was walking home from a friend's apartment on New York's Upper East Side when a man started screaming at him, "What's The frequency, Kenneth?" Rather tried to walk away and as he did the man hit him on the head, knocked him down and started kicking him in the kidneys and neck until passers-by came to the newsman's aid.
The pop group R.E.M. turned the mugging into a popular song called "What's the Frequency, Kenneth" and gossips claimed that Rather's attacker was a jealous husband.
Rather told the Daily News the ugly gossip hurt over the years. "Sometimes it angered me and sometimes it was discouraging," he said.

The newspaper said Tager told a psychiatrist after the NBC murder that he beat Rather and had "contemplated doing worse." Tager had no connection to Rather but did have an uncle in the neighbourhood whom he was visiting when he spotted the newsman.
Tager pleaded guilty to killing the NBC technician. In court papers he said he drove to New York to "take care" of the three major networks, which he said had been out to get him for 20 years.
